title: Möbius Stripped
program_note:
Möbius Stripped was begun in September, 1991, and completed in November of the same year.  While it is scored for six male singers with instrumental accompaniment, the work may be performed a cappella.  If the work is to be performed with accompaniment, however, both the bassoon and the double bass must be used.  The total duration of the work is approximately ten minutes, with the first movement going attacca into the second.  Either movement may be performed individually; if the first movement, “Möbius Stripped”, is performed alone, though, the alternate ending provided at the end of the score should be used.

The titles of each movement, “Möbius Stripped” and “Necker Cubed” are verbal puns but there is a meaningful relation between the titles and the music.  A Möbius Strip is a strip of paper, the ends of which have been joined — after a 180° twist — to form a loop.  It is the twist in the loop which provides, well, “the twist”:  instead of having an inside and an outside a Möbius Strip (or loop) has only one side — or, to put is slightly differently, there is no logical “up or down.”  The musical parallel is harmonic;  while I make use almost exclusively of only four types of chords, all of which are traditionally used in tonal music (major and minor chords, dominant sevenths and minor sevenths), there is no logical up or down — no tonal syntax.  The various harmonies oscillate back and forth (or in bigger or smaller loops), with only voice-leading connections between them.

A Necker Cube is an optical illusion in which the “skeleton” of a cube is presented two dimensionally.  A person may perceive the figure as a depiction of a cube facing down and to one side or as a cube facing up and to the other side — but not both.  There are often, however, psychic “flips” in which the person perceives the cube first one way and then the other.  In this case the musical parallel is rhythmic:  within a particular traditional meter there are other lines which seem to go against the meter, perhaps, or seem syncopated.  The opposing metrical lines grow in strength until, in a rhythmic flip, they are the “proper” meter and it is the other lines which are alien.

David S. Lefkowitz

January 8, 1992

Rochester, NY
